title: Why the Deep Sea Is Full of Giants

paragraphs: In March 2025, a robot six hundred metres beneath the Southern Ocean filmed something nobody had ever seen alive in the wild. A colossal squid.
It was only a baby, about thirty centimetres long. But adults are thought to reach around seven metres, and weigh up to half a tonne. Their eyes are believed to be the largest of any animal alive.

And that's the strange rule of the deep sea. The further down you go, the more often you meet giants. So let's dive. All the way down. To find out why. And to find the invisible line, about eight kilometres down, where even fish give up.
Zero metres. Sunlight, warmth, and life at the size we expect.

But within a few hundred metres, the ocean starts playing with scale. Off the coast of Japan, a crab walks the seafloor on legs that can stretch almost four metres from claw to claw. That's longer than two people lying end to end. The Japanese spider crab is the largest crab alive.
And it's only the beginning.
Two hundred metres. Most of the sunlight is gone. Welcome to the twilight zone.

Here lives a fish that looks like a silver ribbon. The giant oarfish can grow to about eight metres, the longest bony fish on Earth. It has been seen hanging upright in the water, rippling a red fin along its back, like a living banner.

But even the oarfish isn't the longest thing out here. In 2020, explorers in deep canyons off Western Australia came across a siphonophore, coiled into a giant spiral. Its outer ring was estimated at around forty-five metres. That's longer than a blue whale.
And here's the twist. It isn't one animal. It's a colony of countless tiny clones, each with its own job, working together as one body.

One thousand metres. The last of the sunlight is gone. From here down, the only light comes from the animals themselves. The water is close to freezing, and food is rare. Most of it is marine snow, flakes of dead material drifting down from above.
This is where the giants get strange.

In the cold, dark waters of the far north lives the Greenland shark. It can grow over six metres long, but it grows less than a centimetre a year. When scientists carbon-dated the lenses of their eyes, the biggest one came out somewhere between two hundred and seventy-two and five hundred and twelve years old. Even at the low end, it was born before the United States existed.

On the seafloor, you'll find something oddly familiar. A relative of the little woodlouse in your garden, grown to nearly half a metre. The giant isopod. One, at an aquarium in Japan, ate a single fish in January 2009. Then it refused food for five years and forty-three days.
So why are there so many giants down here? Scientists call it deep-sea gigantism. And the honest answer is, there's no single explanation. There are four leading ideas.
One. The cold. Near-freezing water slows everything down. Animals grow slowly, live longer, and keep on growing.
Two. Oxygen. Cold water can hold more of it, and a major study of almost two thousand species of amphipods found that their maximum size rises with oxygen.
Three. Hunger. A bigger body burns less energy per kilogram, and stores more fuel. When your next meal could be months away, size is a survival strategy. Just ask that isopod.
Four. Time. With fewer predators and very long lives, there is simply more time to get big.

But here's what most videos won't tell you. Giants are not the rule down here. Most life on the deep seafloor is tiny, smaller than a millimetre. Gigantism shows up in certain groups, like crustaceans, squid and some fish. The deep doesn't make everything big. It makes a few things enormous.
Six thousand metres. We enter the trenches. The hadal zone, named after Hades. At eight thousand metres, the water pressure is around eight hundred times what you feel at the surface.
And yet, in 2023, scientists revealed footage of a small, pale snailfish swimming at eight thousand, three hundred and thirty-six metres, in a trench off Japan. The deepest fish ever filmed.

It may be about as deep as a fish can go. Fish rely on a molecule called TMAO to keep their proteins working under pressure. Scientists estimate that somewhere between eight thousand two hundred and eight thousand four hundred metres, a fish can no longer hold enough of it.

That's the invisible line. Below it, no fish has ever been found. Only shrimp-like amphipods, other invertebrates and microbes carry on, all the way to the bottom of the Challenger Deep, nearly eleven kilometres down.

And here's the most humbling part. Scientists estimate that we have seen less than a thousandth of one percent of the deep seafloor with cameras. Every giant in this video was found by someone who looked a little deeper than before.
So the real question isn't how big they get. It's what's still down there, that we haven't met yet.
If this dive blew your mind, subscribe. We'll take you somewhere even stranger next time.
